Preamble

Installing games via Lutris is by far the most easiest method available for playing on Linux via Wine.

There are two options available to you:

  • Script Installation
  • Manual installation

Script Installation

Script Installation may sound difficult at first glance, but it really is the easiest method, as pretty much all the work has been done for you, thanks to the User submitted Installation Scripts available on Lutris.net. No scripting on your part required.

Note: Be warned, as these are User submitted scripts, it is entirely the responsibility of the submitter to keep them updated. Game scripts that worked previously, may be broken by future updates, if no one is maintaining them.

Scripts also expect that you have a legitimate copy of a game installer, usually from GOG, or in your Steam account. Each script will state what platform the script is targeting. Do not download a GOG script, for example, if you only own the game on Steam, and vice versa.

Locate the Installation Script

Browser Lutris.net's Game Database for the game you wish to install. Don't worry if it does not exist. If you have access to the installer, you can still setup the game using the manual method.

Here, for example, you can see the entry page for the DOOM 2016 game. It has three install scripts, though all require the use of Steam through Wine.

One script is configured to set the game up to use OpenGL, the other Vulkan, and the last, provides you with the Demo version, configured to use Vulkan as well.

Installing the Game with the Installation Script

Clicking on either of the Install buttons, will launch Lutris and begin the setup process using that particular script. If you click on the drop-down arrow next to Install, you can choose to view the install script, which will show you the YAML file, which will end up in /home/{Your_Username}/.config/lutris/games and tell Lutris how the game is to be configured.

As these scripts are for Steam, the Windows_Steam Runner should be triggered and ask for you to log into your account. Once logged in, the appid included in the script will cause Windows_Steam to begin downloading the required game files.

Note: A GOG install script will work in a similar way, except that it will use plain Wine to run the GOG Install Wizard and setup the game in a Wineprefix.

Manual Installation

If your game does not already have a script, or the script is broken due to lack of maintenance, then you will need to install the game manually.

Using Lutris, this can be done entirely without touching the command line, and here is how.

  1. Launch Lutris (duh)
  2. Click on Game > Add from the menu, or the + icon from the row of icons just below the main menu. This will open the Add New Game window. Make sure Show Advanced Options is ticked, so you can see all the additional configuration options.
  3. Under the Game Info tab, enter a name for the game into the Name field, and the year it was released in the Release Year field.

And now you have a choice to make. Which Runner is going to be used to run the game. If the game requires Steam to install, or run certain features, such as multiplayer, then you would choose Wine_Steam as the Runner. If you're installing a GOG game, or a game with a different sort of installer, you would choose Wine. The steps for both are explained below:

Steam Runner Game Install

To Be Filled In

Wine Runner Game Install

  1. Select Wine as the Runner for the new game install, then switch to the Game Options tab.
  2. Enter a directory path into the Wine Prefix field. This does not need to be a pre-existing folder, as Lutris will create it during Wineboot if it does not exist. Then switch to the Runner Options tab.
  3. Your Wine Runner default setting will be displayed here. Change any that you feel need to be changed to better support the game being installed. For example, using a different Wine Version, if required, configuring certain DLL Overrides, as well as configuring if the game should be launched in a Virtual Desktop (not full screen). You can also enable DXVK from here (more details further in this guide).
  4. Your default System settings will be displayed in the System Options tab. Whether or not you need to modify anything here depends on if your game requires specific fixes or Environment Variables applied. One option that is often required is the checkbox for Reduce PulseAudio Latency, as this will often fix missing or garbled sound in some games.
  5. Click Save to close the window. Your "game" will now appear in the list, but as you may have noticed, we didn't install anything yet, so it is not ready to use. To install the game, right-click on the game's icon in the library list and choose Run EXE inside Wineprefix from the context menu.
  6. Locate the setup.exe for your game and select it. Winetricks will then be used to run the program and install it into the Wineprefix locate you specified under the Game Options tab.
  7. Once the setup program finished, right-click on the game's icon again and choose Configure from the context menu. Return to the Game Options tab and now enter the Working directory and set it to the root folder of where the game was installed inside the prefix.
  8. Lastly, set the Executable to the .exe file used to run the game.

Congratulations, you now have a game installed in Lutris and configured to run in Wine. All that remains is to tweak any additional settings needed by the game for better performance, if you did not do that before running the installer.

Note: You can access Winecfg, Wine Registry, and Joystick Control from the right-click context menu of your game's entry in the Game Library. These will be useful for changing the OS version of Wine, and managing your controllers, if you plan to use one for a game.

DXVK in Lutris

DXVK is available in Lutris and is configured in the Runner Options.

To turn DXVK on, all you need do is check the Enable DXVK checkbox and either leave the default version listed, or enter your own. For example, if you wanted to use the 0.64 release version of DXVK, you would simply enter: 0.64 and Lutris would automatically download that version of DXVK and store it under:

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/lutris/runtime/dxvk

If you wanted to use a non-standard release of DXVK, for example, one which contains a 3rd party patch, you would enter "Manual" under the DXVK Version field, and then place the required folder structure and DLLs under:

/home/{Your_Username}/.local/share/lutris/runtime/dxvk/Manual

You can set DXVK Environment Variables under the System Options tab, such as DXVK_HUD. Just click on Add, then enter DXVK_HUD under the Key column, and set its value (1, fps etc...) in the Value column.
